It also stays open to inspection today, which is the point of the last verse: the sign is the book itself, and anyone can read it.

questions.q: Does the Qur'an contain scientific mistakes?
questions.short: No error has been shown once the Arabic is read properly. The Qur'an is a book of guidance, not a science textbook, and most alleged mistakes come from a poor translation or a forced reading.

points.title: Name the verse first
points.text: Ask which verse and which Arabic word. Many claimed errors vanish once the word's range of meaning is checked in classical dictionaries and tafsir.
points.note: Classical tafsir such as Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari

points.title: A book of guidance
points.text: It calls itself a blessed book to be reflected on and a clarification of guidance. It speaks of the sky, earth and human creation to point to God, not to teach physics.

points.title: It invites investigation
points.text: It tells people again and again to study the universe and themselves, promising the signs will become clear. It does not fear inquiry.

points.title: Facts, not passing theories
points.text: Established facts are weighed against the text, but a changing theory should not overrule it. Clear revelation and sound reason do not truly conflict.
points.note: Ibn Taymiyyah, Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa'l-Naql

points.title: Test one example
points.text: The verse says sun and moon each glide in an orbit. The Arabic verb means to float or glide, not to be fixed in place, which is a fair fit with what we now know, though it is not a lesson in astronomy.

discussion.text: The sceptic points to particular verses and asks why they should not be read at face value. A well-known one says Dhul-Qarnayn found the sun setting in a spring of murky water. Read as a claim about astronomy, that would be a mistake. So the question is whether the Qur'an is making that claim, or describing what a traveller saw.

The first step is to ask what kind of book it says it is. It calls itself a blessed book to be reflected upon, and a clarification of guidance for people who submit. Its verses on the sky, the earth and human creation are given as signs that point to God, not as lessons in physics. Judging it as a textbook is judging it by a standard it never set for itself.

The second step is language. Arabic words often have a range of meaning, and the classical commentators, such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, read many of these verses as describing appearances or events in a story, without ruling on physical fact. Take the sun and moon each moving in an orbit. The verb means to glide or float, which is different from being fixed to a sphere. That is a fair reading; it is not proof that the verse teaches modern astronomy, and nobody should claim more.

The third step is how to weigh science against scripture. Ibn Taymiyyah argued that clear revelation and sound reason cannot truly contradict, so when they seem to, either the reading of the text or the claim of reason is faulty. The sceptic will say that this can protect the text from any test. The reply is that the rule has two sides: a settled fact does push us to re-read a verse, but a passing theory should not overturn the text. The danger to avoid on the other side is forcing every new discovery into a verse after the fact.
discussion.note: Ibn Taymiyyah, Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa'l-Naql

discussion.text: Finally, the book itself does not fear the question. It tells people to look at the universe and at themselves, and promises that the signs will become clear to them. A text that asks for investigation is not behaving like one that is hiding from it. If you have a specific verse in mind, the best course is to bring it, with its Arabic, and look at it on its own terms.

questions.q: If God is perfect, why were some verses abrogated?
questions.short: Abrogation means Allah replaced one ruling with another that fitted a new stage, the way a doctor changes the dose as a patient recovers. He knew both rulings from the start, so it shows complete knowledge, not a mistake. It touches only a few rulings of law, never a belief or a fact about Allah.

points.title: The Qur'an says it happens
points.text: Allah announces that when He replaces a ruling He brings a better one or the like of it, and that He knows best what He sends down.

points.title: New rule, not new knowledge
points.text: Allah knew both rulings from the beginning: the first was meant for one time, the second for what came after. Only His command changes, never His knowledge.

points.title: Hard habits ended in steps
points.text: Drinking was ended in three stages so a deep habit could be left without shock: first its harm is named, then prayer while drunk is barred, then it is banned outright.

points.title: Often it eased the burden
points.text: Muslims were first told to stand against ten times their number. It proved heavy, so Allah lightened it to twice their number. Ibn Abbas explained this in al-Bukhari.

points.title: Few, and known to the Companions
points.text: The prayer direction moved from Jerusalem to the Kaaba, and the Companions turned at once when they were told. Only rulings of law can be abrogated, and the true cases are few.
points.note: al-Suyuti, al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an, chapter on al-nasikh wa'l-mansukh

islamqa.title: Abrogation in the Quran

discussion.text: The objection assumes a perfect God could never change a rule. But changing a rule is not changing knowledge. A father who sets one bedtime for a child of five and another at fifteen knew the whole plan from the start. The Qur'an announces this openly: when Allah replaces a verse or lets it be forgotten, He brings a better one or the like of it. So the change is part of the design, made for people who grow, not an afterthought.

Take drinking. Arabia drank widely, and a ban on day one would have broken many people. The first verse said wine and gambling hold great sin and some benefit. Then believers were told not to pray while drunk. Finally drinking was banned outright. The fasting rule moved the same way: at first those who could fast might instead feed a poor person, then the next verse made fasting the rule for all who are present in the month. Salama ibn al-Akwa reports this in al-Bukhari.

Many changes made life lighter. When Allah first told the believers that twenty steady men would overcome two hundred, it weighed on them, because each had to face ten. Ibn Abbas says Allah then lightened it: a hundred steady men against two hundred. The verse itself says why: He knows there is weakness in you. A sceptic who reads this as fickleness has it backwards. It is the mercy of a Lord who knows the strength of the people He is speaking to.

The clearest example is the direction of prayer. The Prophet prayed toward Jerusalem for about sixteen or seventeen months in Medina, though he longed to face the Kaaba. Then 2:144 came and he turned. Some people mocked, and the Qur'an said the change was a test of who follows the Messenger. When the news reached a mosque of the Ansar in the middle of the afternoon prayer, the whole congregation turned. Nobody at the time saw an error in it.

Honest limits. Abrogation covers commands and permissions only. It never applies to reports, such as what Allah is like, what happened to earlier nations, or what will happen on the Last Day. Scholars also differ on how many cases are real: early writers listed hundreds, but al-Suyuti cut the list to about twenty and Shah Wali Allah to five, because many were only cases where a general rule was narrowed. No verse may be called abrogated by opinion alone; it needs a clear text or agreement.
discussion.note: al-Suyuti, al-Itqan; Shah Wali Allah, al-Fawz al-Kabir

questions.q: Doesn't the Qur'an contradict itself?
questions.short: Every claimed clash so far comes from reading a verse alone: the verses describe different stages, different senses of a word, or different people. The Qur'an itself invites the test, saying that if it were from other than Allah they would find many contradictions in it. Scholars have answered each well-known case.

points.title: The Qur'an invites the test
points.text: It says it is consistent throughout, and that people would find much contradiction in it if it came from anyone but Allah.

points.title: Stages, not clashes
points.text: Man is said to come from dust, clay, water and a drop. These are steps: Adam was formed from earth, and his children from a drop that becomes a clot, then flesh.

points.title: One word, different spans
points.text: In Arabic a 'day' can mean a span of time. A day of a thousand years and a day of fifty thousand years refer to different events, not to two counts of one thing.

points.title: Making, then spreading, the earth
points.text: One passage says the earth was made before the heavens, another says it was spread out after. The answer is that the earth was formed first, then the heavens shaped, then the earth made ready with water and pastures.
points.note: Ibn Abbas' reply on this charge, quoted in al-Bukhari's Tafsir chapter on Surah Fussilat; Ibn Kathir on 79:30

points.title: Do not strike verse with verse
points.text: The Prophet was angry with people who used one part of the Qur'an against another. The clear verses are the base, and the hard ones are read in their light.

islamqa.title: Are There Contradictions in the Quran?

discussion.text: The Qur'an sets its own test. It asks whether people have thought about it, and says that if it were from anyone but Allah they would find in it much contradiction. That is a bold challenge for a book revealed over about twenty-three years, in peace and in war, in Makkah and in Medina, to a man who taught, travelled, fought and ruled in that time. It also calls itself a consistent book, whose parts resemble one another and repeat themes.

Most alleged contradictions are two verses set side by side without their surroundings. For example, one says man was made from dust, another from clay, another from water, another from a drop. Read together they are steps in one process, and the Qur'an shows the steps in order: earth for the first man, then his children from a drop, a clot and flesh. IslamQA's answer goes through several such cases and shows each one fits when the verses are read together.

Another common charge is the order of creation. Surah 41 speaks of the earth in two days, its mountains and food in four, and the heavens in two more. Surah 79 says that after this, Allah spread out the earth. Ibn Abbas was asked exactly this and answered that the earth was made first, then the heavens were shaped, and then the earth was made ready for life. The wording 'after that' in 79:30 is about spreading the earth, not making it.
discussion.note: Ibn Abbas, in al-Bukhari's Tafsir chapter on Surah Fussilat; Ibn Kathir on 41:9-12

discussion.text: A further kind is a general rule followed by an exception, or an earlier ruling replaced by a later one, which is treated in the question on abrogation. Neither is a contradiction; every legal system works this way. The Prophet knew people would misuse the book in arguments. When he found his Companions arguing by setting verses against each other, his face turned red with anger, and he said this was what destroyed the nations before them.

Honest limits. A real contradiction would mean the same subject, the same time and the same sense, and no such case has been shown. Some verses are hard to understand, and scholars have differed on how to read them. The Qur'an itself says some parts are clear and some are less so, and that the clear ones are the base. Not knowing the answer to one verse at once does not turn it into an error. It is where a student goes to a teacher or a tafsir.

topics.title: Miracles of the Qur'an
topics.blurb: Its language, its predictions and history, and why the signs add up to proof.

questions.q: What is the Qur'an's language miracle?
questions.short: The Qur'an challenged the most eloquent people in history to produce even one short surah like it, and they never did, though they had every reason to. Its form is neither poetry nor prose. No attempt since has been accepted as matching it.

points.title: An open challenge
points.text: First to bring a book like it, then ten surahs, then a single surah. The shortest surah, al-Kawthar, is only three short verses.

points.title: Answered in advance
points.text: It said outright 'you will never do it'. One successful surah would have undercut its central claim in public, so the claim was fully exposed to failure.

points.title: The best placed to answer
points.text: Poetry was the Arabs' highest art, and Quraysh were desperate to stop him. They chose war, exile and loss of life over the easy route of composing one surah.

points.title: Neither poetry nor prose
points.text: Opponents tried to call it poetry, magic or soothsaying and could not settle on a label, because it fits none of their known forms. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, a master of verse, could only call it magic.

points.title: So it is not human speech
points.text: Those most able, most motivated and given the most time all failed. If a human could make it, a human could match it. The fitting conclusion is that it comes from God.

islamqa.title: Miraculous aspects of the Holy Qur’an

discussion.text: The strongest objection is that eloquence is a matter of taste. Nobody can measure it, and a challenge judged by believers proves nothing. There is also the thought that Quraysh simply did not bother. The reply starts with who was tested. The challenge was made in public, in Makkah, to the people who lived for the spoken word and who held poetry contests at their markets. The judges were the opponents themselves. They wanted to silence him and had every reason to answer. The bar was also low: a single surah, and the shortest is only three verses.

Now the reasoning, step by step. First, the claim was public and specific: it said they could not do it. Second, failing cost them everything, since he kept winning followers, and succeeding would cost only a few lines of verse. Third, they were known to answer insults with satire, which they did in verse against him. Fourth, they turned to boycott, war and exile instead. The simplest reading is that they tried, or knew better than to try, and could not produce something people would accept. Ibn Kathir makes this argument in his tafsir of 2:23-24, and al-Baqillani builds the case at length in I'jaz al-Qur'an.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir, on 2:23-24; al-Baqillani, I'jaz al-Qur'an

discussion.text: What kind of speech is it? Reports say al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, a respected man of Quraysh, was asked to judge it. He said it was not poetry, not the talk of a soothsayer, and that it had a sweetness to it, yet in the end he settled on 'magic', so as not to have to accept it. The Qur'an records his last word. The point is not this one story, whose chain scholars discuss. It is that the Qur'an has rhyme and rhythm, but no poetic metre, and it is not ordinary prose. The Arabs had no name for it, and it is why the Qur'an says it is neither the word of a poet nor of a soothsayer.

Honest limits. First, this sign can be tested first-hand only by a person who knows Arabic well, so others must rely on those who do. Translation loses it. Second, scholars differed on where the miracle lies. Al-Jurjani (Dala'il al-I'jaz) located it in the arrangement of words, and most scholars agreed. A minority, such as the Mu'tazili al-Nazzam, said God simply turned people away from trying (the 'sarfa' view). Most scholars rejected that, because the text itself is what astonishes. Third, later claimants such as Musaylimah produced rhymed sayings that even his own followers found weak. The claim is not that imitation is logically impossible, but that after fourteen centuries no attempt has been accepted by Arabic speakers as equal.
discussion.note: Al-Jurjani, Dala'il al-I'jaz; al-Baqillani, I'jaz al-Qur'an; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, on Musaylimah

questions.q: Did the Qur'an predict the future?
questions.short: Yes. It made specific claims about events still to come, stated in public, which could have proved it false, and they came true: the Romans' comeback after a crushing defeat, the rout of Quraysh at Badr, and the Muslims entering Makkah.

points.title: A test anyone can run
points.text: A real prediction is specific, made before the event, and could fail. Vague sayings prove nothing; these were none of those.
points.note: Reasoned standard applied to each prediction below

points.title: The Romans would win back
points.text: When Persia had crushed Byzantium, the Qur'an said the Romans would win within a few years (bid', three to nine). Abu Bakr staked a wager on it, first fixing five years, then extending it on the Prophet's advice. Heraclius's counter-attack began within that span.
points.note: Persia took Jerusalem in 614; Heraclius's winning campaign opened in 622. Tirmidhi 3193 records the wager and the extension.

points.title: Quraysh would be routed
points.text: In Makkah, when Muslims were few and weak, it said the gathering would be defeated and turn their backs. At Badr the Prophet went out from his tent reciting this very verse.
points.note: Bukhari 4876: 'A'ishah says this passage was revealed in Makkah while she was a young girl. Bukhari 4877: the Prophet recites it at Badr.

points.title: Makkah would be entered
points.text: After being turned back at Hudaybiyyah, it promised they would enter the Sacred Mosque in safety. They did the next year, then took the city.

points.title: Guesswork cannot explain it
points.text: One wrong prediction would have discredited him before friend and enemy. The ones cited here all came true, which a guesser cannot count on and only the Knower of the unseen can.

islamqa.title: Things foretold in the Quran which have come to pass

discussion.text: The sharpest objection is that prophecy stories are written after the event. If the verses about Rome were composed or adjusted after 622, the whole sign vanishes. A second objection is that the events were guessable. The reply is that a prediction only counts if it is public, specific and dated before the outcome, so each case must pass that test. The Romans case does: the verses are Makkan, the wager was made in public with the idolaters, and the event was checked by everyone who heard about it.

Consider the Roman prediction more closely. In 614 Persia took Jerusalem, and the Roman state looked close to collapse. Gibbon, no friend of Islam, wrote in Decline and Fall (chapter 46) that no prophecy could have seemed more remote from fulfilment at that moment. The verse says the Romans will overcome within 'bid'', which classical scholars gloss as three to nine years. Tirmidhi 3193 shows how honestly the report is kept: Abu Bakr first set five years, lost that term, and was told to extend it. That is not a detail a legend-maker would invent. The tradition also records a second reading of the verse (ghalabat and ghulibat), and Ibn Kathir discusses it in his tafsir of 30:2, while the standard reading is the one used here.
discussion.note: Gibbon, Decline and Fall, ch. 46; Ibn Kathir, Tafsir, on 30:2-4

discussion.text: The Badr case is about weakness. 54:45 is Makkan: A'ishah says in Bukhari that it was revealed when she was a young girl in Makkah, which is when the believers were few and beaten. At Badr, Bukhari 4877 has the Prophet going out of his tent reciting it, with Quraysh in retreat. The Makkah case is softer, because 48:27 was linked to a vision and carries 'if God wills'. Even so, it was said after the setback of Hudaybiyyah, when many companions thought the truce was a humiliation, and it promised a 'conquest near at hand', which scholars such as Ibn Kathir read as Khaybar, then the pilgrimage the next year and the taking of Makkah the year after.

Limits. The sceptic can say that a small number of hits proves little, and that we know the details from Muslim sources. Both are fair. The answer is that the Roman recovery is dated by Byzantine history, not only by Muslim reports, and that the Qur'an itself says these are signs of a Knower of the unseen, not of chance. The argument is cumulative and rests on the standard set in the first point: specific, public, prior, and open to failure.

questions.q: Does the Qur'an know things about history it could not have known?
questions.short: It tells stories of past nations that he, an unlettered man in Makkah, had no way to learn, and says so openly. Its details also fit history where the Bible's differ, such as calling Joseph's ruler a king and Moses's ruler Pharaoh.

points.title: It says he was not there
points.text: After the stories of Mary, Noah and Joseph, it states that he and his people did not know them before. His enemies alleged a human teacher, but never produced one who could account for it.

points.title: King, not Pharaoh, for Joseph
points.text: The Qur'an calls Joseph's ruler 'the king' but Moses's ruler 'Pharaoh'. Egyptians began calling their ruler Pharaoh only in the later era, while the Bible uses Pharaoh for both.
points.note: A fit with Egyptian history, not a proof on its own: Joseph's date is uncertain

points.title: It corrects, not copies
points.text: Where it tells the same stories as earlier books, it differs in key details and clears prophets of faults the Bible gives them. A copier repeats his source.

points.title: No source was in reach
points.text: No Arabic Bible existed then, and he could not read. The knowledge had no human route to him.

points.title: So it came from God
points.text: Knowledge he could not have gained, delivered openly before those who knew his whole life, points to revelation.

discussion.text: The best objection is that he did not need a book. Makkah was a trading town, he travelled to Syria, he met Christians and Jews, and stories travel by mouth. The Qur'an itself records the charge: some said another people helped him, and that these were old legends dictated to him morning and evening. This has to be answered, not waved away. The Qur'an gives its answer inside the same book: the man they pointed to spoke a foreign tongue, while the Qur'an is in clear Arabic.

Ask what the theory needs. The teacher must have existed, known the detailed material, been willing to keep quiet, and taught a man who remained in Makkah among enemies looking for exactly this evidence. Nobody produced him. The reports of contact, such as the monk Bahira or Waraqa ibn Nawfal, are brief, come with chains scholars have questioned, and describe no teaching. Meanwhile, the Qur'an says three times that these accounts were news of the unseen that neither he nor his people had known. A false claim of that kind would be easy to expose in a small town.
discussion.note: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah, on Bahira and Waraqa

discussion.text: The king and Pharaoh detail is a fit, not a proof. Genesis calls Joseph's ruler Pharaoh, but Egyptologists say the word began as 'great house', meaning the palace, and only became a title for the king himself in the New Kingdom, after the age usually assigned to Joseph. The Qur'an says 'the king' for Joseph and 'Pharaoh' for Moses, and keeps that difference. A sceptic may answer that this is chance, and that Joseph's date is itself uncertain. Both points stand. Read alongside the fact that the Qur'an corrects earlier books rather than copying them (for example, Aaron warns against the calf and the blame falls on al-Samiri, and Solomon is cleared of disbelief), the pattern suggests an independent source.
discussion.note: Egyptological usage of 'pr-aa' as a royal title from the New Kingdom; date of Joseph is debated

discussion.text: Limits. Lack of a known source is evidence, not proof, since someone can always say a source was lost. Some sceptics also raise alleged historical errors, and Muslim scholars have written replies to those; a fair reader should weigh them separately. The Qur'an itself also says that it confirms and guards what came before, so overlap is expected. The claim of this argument is narrow: the man had no reachable source, the details fit history where a copier's would not, and this adds to the other signs. Ibn Kathir also warns readers to be careful with unverified stories from earlier peoples.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir, introduction, on Israelite reports

questions.q: Why does the man who brought it matter?
questions.short: The Qur'an came through a man who had never produced poetry or speeches, could not read or write, and was known for honesty. It even reproaches him, and he gained no wealth from it. So he was not a liar, and a deluded man could not have produced it. What remains is that he was truthful and it came from God.

points.title: Forty years of silence
points.text: He lived among his people for forty years before the Qur'an and produced no poetry or oratory. The Qur'an tells them to remember this: they knew his life.
points.note: His everyday speech, recorded in the hadith, reads nothing like the Qur'an.

points.title: He could not read or write
points.text: The Qur'an says he never read a book or wrote one before it, and calls him the unlettered Prophet. That rules out studying earlier writings and writing from them.

points.title: Known as the truthful one
points.text: His people called him al-Amin, the trustworthy. When Heraclius asked Abu Sufyan, then his enemy, whether they had ever accused him of lying before his claim, the answer was no.
points.note: The title al-Amin is from Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah, on the rebuilding of the Ka'bah. Bukhari 7 has Abu Sufyan's 'no'.

points.title: Reproached in his own book
points.text: The Qur'an corrects him in public: for turning from the blind man, for excusing people from battle, over the prisoners of Badr. A forger seeking authority would not write his own faults in. Nor did he gain: he died with his armour pledged for barley.

points.title: Liar, deluded, or truthful
points.text: A liar needs a motive, yet he had no gain, a clean record and a book that shames him. A deluded man could not produce a book that stays consistent and unmatched. Both fail, so the truthful messenger remains.

islamqa.title: Evidence for the truth of the Prophethood of Muhammad

discussion.text: The standard objection is that good character does not prove revelation. Many sincere founders have been honest people who truly believed what they said, and the biography comes from his followers. So the question splits into three: was he lying, was he deluded, and did he write it. The reply takes them in turn, using evidence from the other side where possible. In Bukhari 7, Abu Sufyan, still an enemy, answers Heraclius that they never accused him of lying before his claim, and says he would have lied if he had not feared being called a liar by his own companions. Heraclius drew the conclusion: a man who would not lie about people would not lie about God.
discussion.note: Al-Qadi 'Iyad, al-Shifa', on his character before prophethood

discussion.text: Then the motive. Liars usually gain wealth, power or praise. The Qur'an records him being corrected: for turning away from the blind man, for granting leave to stay behind, over the prisoners of Badr, and over what he hid in himself about Zayd's marriage. A forger writing his own book does not place his mistakes in it. As for wealth, Bukhari 2916 says he died with his armour pledged to a Jew for thirty measures of barley. The Qur'an even says his opponents did not really call him a liar, but rejected the signs. That is the Qur'an's own testimony and is reported, not proven from outside.

Delusion is harder to dismiss with character alone, so the argument uses the book. A deluded person can be sincere, but cannot produce a work that stays consistent for 23 years, includes law, history, argument and prayer, and stays unmatched. His own recorded speech in the hadith is plainly different in style from the Qur'an, and he kept the two apart. Ibn Taymiyya, in al-Jawab al-Sahih, compares true prophets with liars and the possessed, and argues that the difference shows in their message, their conduct, and what follows from them.
discussion.note: Ibn Taymiyya, al-Jawab al-Sahih li-man baddala din al-Masih

discussion.text: On being unlettered, the Qur'an calls him ummi, and 29:48 says he never read or wrote a book before. Most classical scholars, including Ibn Kathir, took this as unable to read and write. Some modern writers say ummi means 'of the gentiles', which would weaken the point, but 29:48 stands on its own words. Honest limit: this argument removes the 'liar' and 'deluded' explanations. It does not by itself prove the Qur'an is revelation. That step comes from putting it together with the other signs.

questions.q: How could a book revealed over 23 years stay consistent?
questions.short: The Qur'an came in pieces over 23 years, through war and peace, grief and victory. Yet it keeps one voice with no contradiction, as it says it would if it were from God. A human author changes over that long and revises his work; there were no drafts here.

points.title: It sets its own test
points.text: It says that if it were from anyone but God, people would find much contradiction in it. Anyone can check that claim.

points.title: Revealed in pieces, to events
points.text: It came in stages, answering events as they happened, not written in one calm sitting.

points.title: No drafts, no revisions
points.text: Each passage was recited as it came, memorised by the companions and written down by scribes. The Prophet was promised he would not forget it. Where a ruling was replaced by a later one, the Qur'an says so openly.

points.title: His own grief stays out
points.text: He wept when his son Ibrahim died, yet no verse mourns him, and when people linked an eclipse to the death he denied it. The deaths of Khadijah and Abu Talib are not lamented either; instead it told him he cannot guide whom he loves.
points.note: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah, on the deaths of Abu Talib and Khadijah

points.title: Why a human could not do it
points.text: Over 23 years a person's mood, views and style shift, and writing shaped by war and grief shows it. Here the voice holds steady and the author's feelings stay out. That points to a source beyond him.

discussion.text: The objection is twofold. First, sceptics list verses they say contradict each other, and the tone of the Makkan and Madinan surahs differs. Second, a careful author could keep a steady line, so consistency proves little. The Qur'an's test is narrow and worded carefully: 'much contradiction', not 'no change of tone'. A book that addresses a persecuted minority and later a ruling community should sound different in its style and topics. The claim is that its teaching on God, judgement, prophets and worship does not change from the first surah to the last.

Apparent conflicts have been treated in works by Muslim scholars for centuries, such as Ibn Qutayba's Ta'wil Mushkil al-Qur'an and al-Shanqiti's Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab. Most turn out to be about different questions, or general and specific statements. Abrogation is a separate case. The Qur'an says openly that God may replace a ruling with another, and the change of rulings on drinking, for example, was done in stages. That is not a slip that got corrected quietly, because it is announced in the text.
discussion.note: Ibn Qutayba, Ta'wil Mushkil al-Qur'an; al-Shanqiti, Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab

discussion.text: Then the circumstances. It came in stages, answering questions, wars, and defeats, and the Qur'an says why: to strengthen his heart. A human writing in those years would show it, and few authors keep their own feelings out of writing for 23 years. Here the speaker is always God addressing him, sometimes consoling him, never voicing his mood. Ibrahim died and he wept, and the Qur'an gave no elegy. An eclipse happened that day, and he refused the crowd's claim that it marked the death, when accepting it would have helped him. Bukhari 1303 and 1043 report both.

Honest limits. Consistency alone is the weakest of the signs, since a skilled author can be consistent. Its force is in combination: consistent over 23 years, produced in changing conditions, without drafts, and still unmatched in language. Silence about his grief is also a negative proof, so it supports the case but cannot carry it. Ibn Kathir, commenting on 4:82, treats the verse as an invitation to reflect and check, and the reader is free to do exactly that.

questions.q: Why do these signs add up to proof?
questions.short: Any one sign could be argued with alone. But they are different in kind and all true together: an unanswered challenge, fulfilled predictions, an unlettered messenger, unbroken consistency, a preserved text and a transformed people. Every other explanation fails on at least one, and only one covers them all: it is from God.

points.title: Signs of different kinds
points.text: The challenge to match it stands unmet. It foretold the Romans' comeback within a few years. It promised its own preservation. It united a people who had been enemies.

points.title: He did not write it himself
points.text: He was unlettered and had produced no such speech in forty years. He was known as honest, and the text reproaches him. Writing it himself leaves no motive and no means.

points.title: No teacher, no copying
points.text: Enemies said a man taught him; the Qur'an answers that the man speaks a foreign tongue while this is clear Arabic. Copying scripture needs reading or a teacher, and both are ruled out.

points.title: One cause fits every sign
points.text: Each other explanation breaks on at least one fact. A human author fails on 23 years of consistency, the unmet challenge and the fulfilled predictions together. Only a source beyond the man accounts for all at once.

points.title: Reflect, then conclude
points.text: The Qur'an does not ask for blind acceptance. It asks people to reflect and promises signs until the truth is clear. Once the alternatives fail, the conclusion is that it is from God.

discussion.text: The fair objection to a cumulative case is that many weak arguments do not add up to a strong one. Zero plus zero is zero. The reply accepts this: the case works only if each sign has real force by itself, and the signs must be different in kind so that one fault cannot sink them all. They are. The challenge is about the text, the Roman prediction is about dated events, the messenger is about a life, the consistency is about how the book was produced, and the union of enemies is about what followed. A rival theory has to explain each of these separately.

Take the rival explanations one at a time. He wrote it: he lacked the means and the motive, and the book reproaches him. He was taught: the accused teacher spoke a foreign tongue, and nobody produced a real source. He was deluded: a delusion does not stay consistent over 23 years or answer a public challenge. It was a group effort: then the group would have answered the challenge in Makkah. It grew as a legend: the text was recited, memorised and written down in his lifetime, and God promises to guard it. Each theory loses on at least one fact, which is why the argument stresses fit with all of them at once.

Why 'from God', and not just 'unexplained'? Because this is reasoning to the best explanation, the way we reason about any past event. When every human explanation fails and the book itself claims a source and gives a test, the source it names becomes the most reasonable remaining answer. Al-Baqillani argued in I'jaz al-Qur'an that the proof is the combination of the inimitable text and the claim it makes. A closed mind can always say 'we do not know yet', and that remains possible. But the Qur'an asks people to weigh the evidence for themselves, so the conclusion is offered, not forced.

Limits, said plainly. No historical claim can be proven the way a chemistry experiment can. The standard here is the one we accept for any past event: what a fair person can reasonably conclude from the evidence. The Qur'an itself notes that some who see the signs still reject them, and asks whether their hearts are locked. It also records people demanding other signs. So the signs give a strong reason to believe, and the last step of honest reflection is left to the reader.

topics.title: Violence and Jihad
topics.blurb: Was Islam spread by the sword, and what does jihad mean?

questions.q: Wasn't Islam spread by the sword?
questions.short: No. Armies did expand Muslim rule, but the Qur'an forbids forcing belief, and most people came to Islam over generations through trade, teaching and example. Most Muslims today live where no Muslim army ever went.

points.title: Belief cannot be forced
points.text: There is no compulsion in religion; the Prophet's job was to convey, not to control hearts.

points.title: Conquest is not conversion
points.text: Jews and Christians kept their faith under Muslim rule for centuries, paying a tax in place of military service. That is impossible if conversion was forced.
points.note: Christian and Jewish communities of Egypt, Syria and Iraq to this day

points.title: Fighting had set reasons
points.text: Fighting was permitted against those who attacked or expelled Muslims or blocked the message by force, never for disagreeing.

points.title: Many were never conquered
points.text: Indonesia, Malaysia and large parts of East and West Africa came to Islam largely through merchants and teachers, not through an invading army.
points.note: Richard Bulliet, Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period

points.title: Invitation first, always
points.text: Commanders had to invite people and offer terms before fighting, and spare women and children. Scholars who say the sword removed obstacles still held that no one is made to believe.

islamqa.title: Was Islam spread by the sword?

discussion.text: The strongest form of the objection is a timeline. Within about a century of the Prophet's death, Muslim armies held Syria, Egypt, Iraq, Iran, North Africa and Spain. Armies clearly moved. So the sceptic asks: if the Qur'an says there is no compulsion, why did the map change so fast? The answer starts by pulling apart two things the question joins together: expanding a state, and changing what people believe.

On belief, the Qur'an speaks directly. It tells the Prophet he is only a reminder, not a controller over people, and asks whether he would compel people to believe. Ibn Kathir, in his commentary on 2:256, explains that faith has to be accepted by the heart, so forcing it would be meaningless. One reported occasion for the verse is in Abu Dawud: some Ansar parents had raised children as Jews, and when Banu al-Nadir were expelled they wanted to keep them. The verse was revealed and they were not forced.

The conduct of conquest points the same way. Rulers who wanted everyone converted would not have set a tax for Jews and Christians to keep their faith, yet 9:29 does exactly that. Critics rightly notice the phrase 'while they are humbled', which describes a lower civic status, and it should be admitted. But it is a status inside a system that let them stay. The Qur'an even names their churches and synagogues as places God protects by checking people through one another. Richard Bulliet's study of conversion estimated that in places like Iran a majority became Muslim only after roughly two centuries. A slow curve like that fits gradual choice, not a sword held over each person.
discussion.note: Richard Bulliet, Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period

discussion.text: What about the hadith where commanders offer three options: Islam, the tax, or fighting? Many classical jurists took this to allow campaigns that bring lands under Muslim rule. Ibn Taymiyya, in al-Siyasa al-Shar'iyya, argued that the reason for fighting is being at war, not disbelief, which is why women, monks and the elderly who do not fight are protected. Either way, the option to keep one's religion under treaty stayed open. Even the wider view is a claim about who governs, not a claim that a person may be made to believe.

Honest limits: rulers were human. Some episodes did involve pressure or force, such as the Almohad persecution of Jews in twelfth century Spain and North Africa, and taxes and social advantage pushed many people toward Islam. Scholars judge coercion of that kind to be against the religion. The claim is not that nobody ever converted under pressure. It is that the law forbids forcing belief, and that most conversion came gradually through trade, teaching and example.

questions.q: Doesn't jihad mean holy war against non-Muslims?
questions.short: No. Jihad means striving, and most of it is peaceful: against your own desires, with words, with wealth. Armed fighting is one form, bound by strict rules, and never a licence to attack people for not being Muslim.

points.title: It means striving
points.text: The word comes from juhd, effort. The Qur'an uses it for doing good, patience and defending the faith.

points.title: Peaceful jihad came first
points.text: In Makkah, before any fighting, God told the Prophet to strive with the Qur'an: a great striving by argument and patience.

points.title: Many forms, not one
points.text: Scholars list jihad against the self, against Shaytan, with words and with wealth, as well as fighting.

points.title: Fighting has strict limits
points.text: Armed jihad is a communal duty under legitimate authority, only against those who fight. Killing women, children and non-combatants is forbidden.

points.title: Not war on all unbelievers
points.text: God does not forbid kindness and fairness to peaceful non-Muslims.

islamqa.title: Ruling on jihad and kinds of jihad

discussion.text: The objection at its strongest: in the fiqh manuals, the chapter called Kitab al-Jihad is mostly about fighting, so 'holy war' looks like a fair translation of the technical term. That is true of the manuals. But the manuals use the word in its narrow legal sense, and the Qur'an and hadith use it far more widely. A fair reader has to hold both: the word means striving, and one branch of it is armed fighting under rules.

There is a simple test for whether 'striving' is meant. The Qur'an tells the Prophet to strive against the disbelievers 'with it', meaning the Qur'an, a great striving. That verse was revealed in Makkah. Fighting was only permitted later, after the migration to Madinah, when 22:39 gave permission to those being attacked. So in Makkah the word cannot have meant fighting. It meant argument, patience and steadfastness under persecution.

The hadith show the same range. A man asks to join the fighting and the Prophet asks whether his parents are alive, then tells him to strive in serving them. Another report says the best jihad is a just word to an oppressive ruler. Another tells believers to strive against the polytheists with their wealth, their persons and their tongues. Ibn al-Qayyim, in Zad al-Ma'ad, sets out the levels of jihad and places striving against one's own self first.

One popular saying should be avoided: that the Prophet returned from battle and said 'we return from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad.' Many hadith scholars, including Ibn Taymiyya, judged it to have no sound basis. The argument here does not need it, since the Qur'an and sound hadith already show the wide meaning. Nor should the narrow meaning be played down. Armed jihad is a real duty in Islamic law, but a communal one: if enough people take it up, the rest are relieved of it, as Ibn Qudama explains in al-Mughni.

Nuance and limits: scholars have disagreed over whether armed jihad may be offensive or only defensive. Classical scholars mostly allowed campaigns by a legitimate state, and many modern scholars restrict it to defence. On both views the tradition's own conditions matter: lawful authority, a fight only against those who fight, no transgression. That is why a self-declared 'jihad' by a private group fails the test, however it describes itself.

questions.q: Doesn't the Qur'an say 'kill the unbelievers wherever you find them'?
questions.short: That verse (9:5) is about the Arabian polytheists who broke their treaties and attacked the Muslims, not non-Muslims in general. The same passage spares those who kept treaties and protects anyone who asks for safety.

points.title: Read the verses around it
points.text: 9:4 exempts those who kept their treaties, and 9:13 names the target: those who broke oaths, tried to expel the Prophet and attacked first.

points.title: Asylum is commanded
points.text: If any polytheist asks for protection, grant it, let him hear the Qur'an, then escort him to safety.

points.title: No compulsion still stands
points.text: 9:5 is a wartime ruling about one enemy; it does not cancel 'no compulsion in religion'.

points.title: Fight back, don't start
points.text: Fight only those who fight you, and do not go beyond the limit.

points.title: Peace answers peace
points.text: If the enemy leans to peace, accept it. Peaceful non-Muslims are owed justice and kindness.

islamqa.title: Specious argument from a Christian who claims that there are verses in the Qur'an which contradict the verse {There shall be no compulsion in [acceptance of] the religion} [al-Baqarah 2:256]

discussion.text: Read alone, 9:5 sounds unqualified: kill the polytheists wherever you find them, and if they repent, establish prayer and pay zakah, let them go. A sceptic will say that reads as 'convert or die'. That deserves a real answer, not a dismissal, and the answer is in the verses around it.

The chapter opens by ending treaties with certain polytheists. Then 9:4 exempts those who kept their treaty and did not help anyone against the Muslims. 9:7 says that as long as those at the Sacred Mosque are upright, the Muslims must be upright. 9:13 gives the reason for the fighting: a people who broke their oaths, meant to expel the Messenger and attacked first. In the same year, an announcement was made at Hajj that no polytheist would perform Hajj after that year. The audience is the Arab tribes of that time who had fought the Muslims for years, not all non-Muslims for all time. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it this way.

What about the 'repent' clause? For those treaty-breakers the passage offers three routes: keep or make a treaty, ask for protection, or join the community. The verse right after 9:5 closes the loop: a polytheist who asks for protection is protected, hears God's words, and is then escorted to his place of safety. Nothing in that says he must accept Islam first. Hearing is not believing, and he leaves safe whatever he decides. That is the opposite of convert or die.

The second challenge is abrogation. Some early commentators, listed in abrogation works such as al-Suyuti's al-Itqan, said 9:5 cancelled earlier verses about forgiving and turning away. If so, a sceptic can say extremists have classical support. That is a fair point: such readings exist in the books. But a ruling about belief cannot be cancelled by a ruling about one war, and IslamQA holds that 9:5 does not cancel 2:256. Most scholars therefore read the verses of restraint and peace as still in force.

The last test is consistency across the Qur'an. It says to fight those who fight you but not to transgress. It allows retaliation only in proportion. If the enemy leans to peace, accept it. And it says God does not forbid kindness and justice toward those who do not fight you over religion. A reading of 9:5 that contradicts all of these is a worse reading than one that places it in its wartime setting.

questions.q: Why do Muslims commit terrorism?
questions.short: Islam forbids killing innocents, and scholars across the schools call attacks on civilians a major sin. Anyone who does it is breaking the religion, not following it.

points.title: One life is all humanity
points.text: Killing one innocent person is like killing all people; saving one is like saving all.

points.title: Civilians are protected
points.text: The Prophet forbade killing women and children in war, and said whoever kills a non-Muslim under a treaty will not smell Paradise.

points.title: Even scaring is forbidden
points.text: A Muslim may not frighten another even as a joke. Terror against innocents is far worse.

points.title: Spreading terror is punished
points.text: The Qur'an sets its harshest penalty for those who wage war on society and spread corruption.
points.note: Ibn Kathir on 5:33; the Amman Message (2004)

points.title: Crimes are personal
points.text: A Muslim's crime is his own, not his religion's. Most victims of groups like ISIS have been Muslims.

islamqa.title: Definition of terrorism and what it means in Islam and in the West

discussion.text: The objection at its strongest: attackers say they act for Islam, quote verses and use its vocabulary, so surely the religion gives them something. The way to test that is to ask what the tradition itself permits, not what a group claims. Take terrorism to mean deliberately attacking civilians to frighten a public. On that definition the sources say no, clearly and repeatedly.

In the Qur'an, killing one soul unjustly is compared with killing all of humanity. The verse is addressed to the Children of Israel, but commentators treat it as a general principle, and it is placed among the Qur'an's rules about human life. Elsewhere the Qur'an forbids killing the soul God has made sacred 'except by right', which in law means by a court's process, not by private decision. Deliberately killing a believer is threatened with Hell.

The hadith apply this to war itself. The Prophet forbade killing women and children, and warned that whoever kills a person under treaty with the Muslims will not smell the fragrance of Paradise. Another report says it is not lawful for a Muslim to frighten another Muslim. Abu Bakr's instructions to his commander, recorded by Malik in the Muwatta, forbade killing children, women and the old, cutting down fruit trees, or harming monks in their retreats. That report has a broken chain but is widely cited by jurists.

Islamic law even has a category for this crime. 5:33 sets the harshest penalties for those who wage war on society and spread corruption. Jurists applied it to armed bands who terrorise roads and cities, and it is handled by a court. In that framework, a group that kills civilians is not a holy army but a criminal one. The Amman Message of 2004 and 2005, backed by hundreds of scholars, was also aimed at takfir, declaring other Muslims to be unbelievers, which extremist groups use as licence to kill them.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir on 5:33; the Amman Message (2004)

discussion.text: Honest limits: there are real gaps to admit. A hadith records the Prophet being asked about night raids that might expose women and children to harm, and he said 'they are from them.' Later jurists read that as covering unintended harm when a lawful military target is attacked, not deliberate targeting, but extremists have quoted such reports out of context. Modern scholars also argue over what counts as lawful resistance. Still, no classical school allows deliberately killing civilians, and each person answers for his own act. Most victims of groups like ISIS have been Muslims.

questions.q: Is it true that Muslims who leave Islam are killed?
questions.short: In the classical ruling of all four Sunni schools, a Muslim who knowingly and freely leaves Islam may be executed, but only by a court and only after repentance is offered. Some modern scholars limit it to apostasy joined with treason.

points.title: The classical ruling
points.text: The hadith says 'Whoever changes his religion, kill him', and the four schools took it as a state penalty.

points.title: Repentance offered first
points.text: The person is asked to repent, often over three days, and helped with doubts before any penalty.

points.title: Only a court, not individuals
points.text: Penalties belong to the judge and the state. A private person who kills for this commits murder.
points.note: The fiqh manuals on who carries out hudud

points.title: The Qur'an names no worldly penalty
points.text: It condemns leaving Islam and warns of the Hereafter, but sets no punishment in this life.

points.title: A political side is debated
points.text: The hadith describes one who leaves the community. Scholars like al-Qaradawi therefore apply it only to apostasy that attacks the community.
points.note: Yusuf al-Qaradawi; a minority view in classical fiqh

islamqa.title: Punishment for Apostasy in Islam

discussion.text: The objection at its strongest: this appears to contradict 'no compulsion in religion.' If a person may be killed for changing belief, then faith is being kept in place by threat. That is a serious challenge, and the honest first step is to state the classical ruling as it stands. The four Sunni schools held that a Muslim who knowingly and freely leaves Islam may face execution, after repentance is offered, and only by a court.

The evidence for it is the hadith 'whoever changes his religion, kill him.' A second report gives the permitted grounds for taking a Muslim's life as three: a life for a life, the married adulterer, and one who leaves his religion and abandons the community. The majority took the last clause as describing the act itself, since leaving the faith is leaving the community. A minority, including al-Qaradawi in our time, took it as a condition: apostasy joined with betrayal or fighting the community. Both readings rest on the same text, which is why the disagreement is real.

Two pieces of practice pull toward caution. A bedouin gave the Prophet his pledge, fell ill in Madinah and asked to cancel it. The Prophet refused three times, and the man left the city. No punishment is recorded. Classical scholars did not treat this as cancelling the ruling. And Umar, on hearing that a man had been killed after apostasy without delay, said he should have been held three days and fed bread each day, so he might repent. That is why repentance is offered first, and some early jurists such as al-Nakha'i and al-Thawri held it should be offered for as long as it takes, as reported by Ibn Hajar in Fath al-Bari.
discussion.note: Malik, al-Muwatta, Book of Judgments; Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari

discussion.text: The Qur'an itself repeatedly condemns leaving the faith and warns of the Hereafter, but never sets a punishment in this world. One verse says a person forced to say words of disbelief while his heart is secure in faith is excused, so the law needs proof that the person chose freely and knew what he was doing. That is a high bar for any court.

Honest limits: the majority classical position is what it is, and IslamQA states it. The minority view is respectable but is a minority, and some Muslim-majority states still have laws on the subject. What can be said with confidence is that no individual may carry it out, that a private killing is murder, and that the Qur'an sets out its own consequences for leaving faith in the Hereafter. A sceptic may still find the ruling hard, and it is better to say so plainly.

topics.title: Women in Islam
topics.blurb: Equality, hijab, inheritance, and the verses people quote.

questions.q: Doesn't Islam oppress women?
questions.short: No. Islam gave women the right to own property, inherit, trade and learn 1,400 years ago, and ranks mothers first in honour. Where women are mistreated today, people are failing Islam, not following it.

points.title: Equal before God
points.text: Men and women are addressed equally in faith, worship and reward. Each is judged on their own deeds.

points.title: Mothers ranked highest
points.text: Kindness to parents is tied to worship of God. The Prophet named the mother three times before the father, and said Paradise is at her feet.

points.title: Rights as wives
points.text: Wives have rights like their duties, and the marriage gift is hers alone. The Prophet said the best of you are the best to their wives.

points.title: Her own wealth
points.text: A woman owns, earns, trades and inherits in her own name. No husband or father may take it without her consent.

points.title: Daughters are a blessing
points.text: Islam ended the burying of baby girls. The Prophet promised closeness to him for whoever raises daughters well.

islamqa.title: Women's Rights in Islam

discussion.text: The strongest form of this objection is not about a single rule. It is about the overall picture: in many Muslim-majority countries women face limits on education, work or movement, so surely the religion is the cause. A fair answer starts by separating two questions: what does the source text establish, and what do societies do in its name? The Qur'an addresses believing men and believing women side by side, promising both forgiveness and a great reward, and says that no deed of a doer, male or female, is lost. Spiritually, then, the two stand in the same place before God.

The second step is to compare with the world in which the message came. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir of 4:7, record that women and children had commonly been left out of inheritance in pre-Islamic Arabia. Against that background, a verse giving women a fixed and named share of what parents and relatives leave was a real change, and the Qur'an also says that women have a share in what they earn. The bride's marriage gift is hers to keep, and a woman's property does not merge into her husband's.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on 4:7

discussion.text: Third, the honour given to mothers is unusually specific. A man asked the Prophet who deserved his best company, and he answered 'your mother' three times before saying 'your father'. Another companion wanted to go out to fight, and the Prophet sent him back to look after his mother, telling him to stay with her because Paradise is beneath her feet. Kindness to parents is placed right after the worship of God in the Qur'an, and the verse names the hardship of old age directly.

Marriage and daughters follow the same pattern. The Prophet said the best of you is the best to his wives, and added that he was the best of them to his wives. The Qur'an condemns burying baby girls, and the Prophet said whoever raises two girls well will be close to him on the Day of Resurrection.

The honest limit is this: a text cannot prevent a person from ignoring it. Where women are denied inheritance, schooling or a say in marriage, a Muslim can and should point to these rulings as the standard being broken. A sceptic is right to judge Muslims by how they behave, and right to expect Muslims to hold themselves to the standard. The claim here is narrower: the source itself does not teach the oppression, and that is checkable by reading the verses and reports above.

questions.q: Why do Muslim women have to cover?
questions.short: A Muslim woman covers first because God commanded it, as obedience and modesty. The Qur'an gives the wisdom: she is recognised as dignified and protected from harassment, and men are commanded to be modest first.

points.title: A command from God
points.text: The Qur'an tells believing women to draw their head covers over their chests. A believer obeys out of trust, even before seeing every reason.

points.title: Dignity and protection
points.text: Covering makes women known as respectable, so they are not harassed.

points.title: Men are commanded first
points.text: The verse telling men to lower their gaze and guard their modesty comes right before the one for women. The duty is shared.

points.title: Worship, not force
points.text: No one can be forced to believe. Once a person believes, covering is one of the commands they follow willingly, and millions wear it by conviction. Obedience comes first, understanding the wisdom second.

islamqa.title: Why Do Women Cover Their Hair?

discussion.text: The strongest objection is that a rule about clothing cannot be fair if it applies to one sex more visibly than the other, and that a woman's dignity should not depend on cloth. The first step in reply is to be clear what the Muslim claim actually is. It is not that a woman is unsafe or dishonourable without it. It is that God commanded it, and a believer obeys a command from God whose wisdom they trust, in the same way as with prayer or fasting. The verse tells believing women to wrap their head covers over their chests.

Second, the early community understood it as a clear command. Aisha reported that when this verse was revealed, the early emigrant women tore their wrappers and covered themselves with them right away. Classical scholars of all four schools, such as Ibn Kathir in his tafsir on 24:31, took the head covering as required, and the disagreement among them was about how much of the face and hands may show, not about the head.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on 24:31

discussion.text: Third, the sceptic says it is unfair to women alone. But the verse for men comes first and commands them to lower their gaze and guard their private parts. Both sexes have a modesty code; the forms differ. Also, the Qur'an gives a reason for the outer garment: that women 'will be known and not be abused'. The wisdom is stated as recognition and protection, and the reader should notice that the burden of restraint is placed on the man first.

Fourth, the word 'force'. The verse 'no compulsion in religion' says that no one can be made to believe, and it does not by itself settle every question about dress. What follows from it is that faith has to be freely chosen, and worship that is forced is not worship. Once someone chooses Islam, they are held to its commands, as with any faith. It follows that a woman made to wear it by a family or a state is not doing what the Qur'an describes, and many scholars say so.

The honest limit is that this reasoning explains what Muslims believe; it cannot make an outsider agree that the command is right. There is also a rule that shows it is not about shame: elderly women past marriage are told there is no blame on them for putting aside their outer garments, though modesty is better for them. That shows a rule about modesty and the setting of a limit, not a claim that a woman's body is a fault.

questions.q: Why does a woman inherit half of what a man does?
questions.short: In some cases a woman gets half a brother's share, because only the man must pay for the family. She spends on no one and keeps all she has, so she is not worse off. Other shares are equal, and some favour her.

points.title: A fixed ruling
points.text: God set the shares in the Qur'an, including a son receiving two daughters' shares. It is not a claim that women are worth half.

points.title: Not always half
points.text: Mother and father each get one sixth when there is a child, and siblings through the mother share equally.

points.title: Men carry the costs
points.text: The husband pays the marriage gift, housing and upkeep, and supports relatives. That duty is the reason for the larger share.

points.title: Her money is hers
points.text: A wife has no duty to spend on the household, even if she is rich. Anything she gives is voluntary and rewarded.

points.title: Compare the result
points.text: Her share is kept entirely for herself, while his is largely spent on others.

islamqa.title: Women's Inheritance Share Unchanged by Household Spending

discussion.text: The strongest form of this objection: in a fair system, equal persons get equal shares, so 'a male gets the share of two females' looks like a plain statement that a woman is worth half. The first step is to read what the verse says and does not say. It names the son-and-daughter case, and it is one case among several. A daughter alone gets half the estate; two or more daughters get two thirds; a mother and a father each get a sixth when the deceased leaves a child.

Second, the equal cases are real. A brother and a sister from the same mother each get a sixth, and if there are more they share a third equally. So the rule is not 'women inherit half'. Scholars of inheritance list many situations where a woman receives the same as a man or more. The half applies mainly where a son and a daughter of the deceased inherit together, or siblings of the same parents.

Third, the reason offered by scholars is about who must spend, not who is worth more. The Qur'an makes the husband responsible for the marriage gift and for maintenance, and this duty stays with him even if the wife is wealthy. The Qur'an says men are in charge of women 'by what they spend from their wealth'. A brother's larger share arrives with duties towards a wife, children, and often parents or relatives, while a sister's share arrives with no such duty. She may spend it however she likes.

Fourth, the argument tested at its hardest. Suppose a brother has no dependants and a sister has children. Then the rule does not track need in that case. The reply is that Islamic law sets fixed shares by general categories, so that the family is not turned into a court case over every household, and the sister's own protection lies in the maintenance duty that falls on her husband or her male relatives. A rule that works in the typical case can feel unfair in a hard case; the scholars accept that as the price of a fixed share.
discussion.note: Classical fiqh of fara'id; see Ibn Qudamah, al-Mughni, Book of Inheritance

discussion.text: The honest limit is that this is a ruling a Muslim accepts because God set the shares, and then finds the wisdom in it; the wisdom above is the classical explanation, not the reason the ruling is binding. A sceptic may still think the fixed ratio ignores modern households where women earn and pay. The fair reply is that her money remains hers in either case, and a woman who chooses to spend on her family is doing an act of charity that is rewarded.

questions.q: Doesn't 4:34 allow husbands to beat their wives?
questions.short: The verse deals with a wife's serious misconduct, in steps: advise, then separate beds, and at most a light tap that leaves no pain or mark, which scholars say is better left. The rule of marriage is kindness, and the Prophet never struck a woman.

points.title: Kindness is the rule
points.text: Live with wives honourably; the best of you are the best to their wives.

points.title: Steps, for serious wrong
points.text: The verse starts with advice, then leaving the bed. It is for serious misconduct, not everyday quarrels.

points.title: No harm allowed
points.text: In his farewell sermon the Prophet allowed only a strike that is 'not severe', in the case of a wife letting in someone he dislikes. Ibn Abbas is reported to have said: like with a toothstick, causing no pain or injury.

points.title: The Prophet's own example
points.text: Aisha said he never struck a woman or a servant. Al-Shafi'i said leaving it is better.

points.title: Other ways out
points.text: If the marriage is failing, family arbitrators step in, and a wife may ask to end it: the Prophet approved the wife of Thabit ibn Qays ending her marriage by returning the garden she had been given.

islamqa.title: Beating Wife in Islam

discussion.text: This is the hardest verse in the topic for a sceptic, and it should be met directly. The verse says that if a husband fears arrogance or persistent ill-conduct in his wife, he should advise her, then leave her bed, and then 'strike' her. Read alone, and in English, it sounds like a licence for violence. The first step is to read it in the setting of the surrounding verses. Just before, the Qur'an tells husbands to live with their wives in kindness, and the Prophet said the best of you is the best to his wives.

The second step is the order of the verse: advice, then separation in bed, and only then the third step. The steps rise in seriousness, and the classical commentators, such as Ibn Kathir, treat the third as a last measure, only for real misconduct and never for everyday quarrels. Al-Tabari records Ibn Abbas and others explaining the strike as one that leaves no mark, comparable to a light touch with a toothstick. Ibn Kathir also records that Imam al-Shafi'i held that leaving it altogether is better.
discussion.note: al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan, and Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on 4:34

discussion.text: Third, the Prophet's own conduct sets the practical meaning. Aisha said he never struck anyone with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant, except when fighting in God's cause. In the farewell pilgrimage report, the only strike mentioned is one that is 'not severe', in the context of a wife letting into the home someone the husband dislikes. The sceptic should notice that the same report also lists the husband's duties to feed and clothe her fairly.

Fourth, the verse is not the only route. If the marriage is in serious trouble, the Qur'an tells both families to send an arbitrator each, and promises that God will bring about agreement if both want it. A wife also has a path out: in the report of Thabit ibn Qays's wife, she asked to end the marriage, the Prophet accepted her returning the garden he had given her, and told him to accept it and separate. Abuse is never described as a right of the husband.

The honest limit: the word in the verse is a strike, and scholars have differed on how to understand it, with some saying it must be a symbolic touch and others noting that the safest opinion is to avoid it. Anyone who uses this verse to justify harming a wife is going against the Prophet's own example and the limits the scholars set, and nothing here excuses domestic abuse.

questions.q: Why can a Muslim man have four wives?
questions.short: It is permitted, not required, and only with justice. The Qur'an capped it at four when Arabia had no limit, and says marry one if you fear being unfair.

points.title: Limited, not invented
points.text: Before Islam men took any number of wives. The Qur'an capped it at four and tied it to justice.

points.title: Justice is the condition
points.text: If a man fears he cannot be fair, he must marry one. He must never neglect a wife by leaning wholly to another.

points.title: It protected the vulnerable
points.text: The verse opens with orphan girls: Aisha explained that a guardian might marry a girl in his care for her wealth without a fair gift, and God told him to marry other women instead. The surah was revealed after Uhud, when many women were left without a provider.

points.title: Women keep their rights
points.text: A woman may refuse such a marriage, and in the Hanbali school she can make monogamy a condition of her contract. Each wife keeps her own home, upkeep and gift.

points.title: Trust the ruling
points.text: A believer accepts God's ruling even where it is hard, since good may lie in what we dislike.

islamqa.title: Why Allah Permits Polygamy Even Though It Hurts the Wife's Feelings

discussion.text: The strongest objection is that a man having several wives treats women as things to be collected, and that no wife can be content sharing her husband. It should be granted at once that many women find it painful, and IslamQA itself says the wife's feelings are real. The reply starts from what the verse actually says. It does not say 'marry four'. It begins with a concern for orphan girls and says: if you fear you will not deal justly, then marry one. The default is one, and more is a permission with a condition attached.

Second, the setting. Aisha, in the report in Sahih al-Bukhari, explained that the verse was about an orphan girl in the care of a guardian who wanted to marry her for her wealth and beauty without giving her a fair marriage gift. God told such men to marry other women instead. Many commentators also connect the surah to the aftermath of the battle of Uhud, when many men had died and many women and children needed care. That link comes from later commentary, so it is a likely setting rather than a proven cause.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on 4:3

discussion.text: Third, the limit and the condition. Before Islam, reports say men could marry without a set limit, and the verse fixed the ceiling at four. The condition is justice, and the Qur'an is honest about how hard it is: you will never be able to be fully equal in feeling, so do not incline completely toward one and leave the other hanging. Scholars read this as equality in what can be controlled, such as time, housing and spending, not in love.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on 4:3

discussion.text: Fourth, the woman's position. She cannot be married without her consent. The Prophet said a woman previously married must be consulted, and a virgin must give her permission, which her silence may show. In the Hanbali school, as Ibn Qudamah records in al-Mughni, a woman may make it a condition of her marriage contract that her husband takes no other wife, and the condition is binding. Each wife has her own marriage gift and her own right to upkeep.

The honest limit: this is a permission, not a virtue, and no text says it is better than one wife. Most Muslim marriages today are to one wife. A believer accepts it because it is in the Qur'an, trusting that good may lie in what we dislike; a sceptic will weigh the argument differently, and the question of whether a man will in fact act justly is where abuse most often occurs.

questions.q: Why is a woman's testimony worth half a man's?
questions.short: The half-witness rule appears in one verse, about writing down a loan, and it gives its own reason: if one woman errs or forgets, the other reminds her. It is a safeguard for a written record, not a claim that women are less honest. Elsewhere a woman's word is accepted alone, and a wife's oath weighs the same as her husband's.

points.title: One verse, one setting
points.text: The rule of a man and two women is in the verse on writing loan contracts. The Qur'an does not give it as the rule for all testimony.

points.title: The reason is given
points.text: It says why: so that if one errs, the other can remind her. The concern is memory and error, not honesty. IslamQA adds that this describes a general pattern, not every woman.

points.title: Equal weight elsewhere
points.text: In the oaths between spouses when a husband accuses his wife, her sworn word stands against his and cancels the penalty.

points.title: A woman's word alone
points.text: When a woman said she had nursed both spouses, the Prophet took her word alone, and Uqba separated from his wife. Where women know best, one is enough.

points.title: Worth is measured by piety
points.text: Honour before Allah is measured by piety. The Prophet told a man that his mother has three times the claim on his good company.

islamqa.title: Why is the witness of one man considered to be equal to the witness of two women?

discussion.text: Look first at how narrow the rule is. The Qur'an mentions two women in place of one man in one place only: the long verse on writing down a debt that runs for a fixed time. It says to call in two witnesses from your men, or if two men are not there, a man and two women, of those whom you accept as witnesses. This is not a statement on all evidence in every court, and it is not a ranking of men over women.

The verse gives its reason in the same sentence: so that if one of the two women errs, the other can remind her. The word is about error and forgetting, not lying. IslamQA explains that the memory of two women takes the place of the memory of one man, and notes this is a general pattern, since some women are stronger than many men. Two women make the record safer. The Qur'an also says believing men and women get the same forgiveness and reward.

The hardest text is a hadith from the Eid sermon, where the Prophet points to this rule as the meaning of a 'deficiency in intelligence'. A modern reader may wince at the words, and it is fair to say so. Scholars such as al-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar explain it as a weaker hold on details in that one setting, and not a lack of ability or honesty, just as the exemption from prayer during a period is a mercy, not a fault. In the same sermon he urged the women to give in charity.
discussion.note: al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim; Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, on the hadith of women's deficiency

discussion.text: The half rule is not applied everywhere. In matters women handle themselves, such as birth and nursing, one woman's word is accepted alone; the Prophet did so in the case of Uqba ibn al-Harith. A wife's oath stands equal to her husband's. And in the religion itself, a woman like Aisha is trusted alone as a transmitter of hadith, and much of the Sunnah on private life comes through women.
discussion.note: al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, on Aisha as a narrator

discussion.text: Honest limits. The schools differ on which cases need men only, such as the fixed penalties, and which allow women's evidence. Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim argued that a judge should accept any proof that shows the truth, including one honest witness or clear signs, because the aim of the law is justice. So the half rule is a default for certain documents, not a limit on how truth is found. The verse on witnessing also asks all witnesses to give evidence justly, even against themselves.

questions.q: Why can a Muslim man marry a Christian woman but not the reverse?
questions.short: A Muslim man already honours the prophets and scriptures of Jews and Christians as part of his faith, so her religion is safe in his home. A non-Muslim husband does not honour Muhammad or the Qur'an, and the husband leads the household, so a Muslim woman's faith and her children's would be at risk. Scholars agree on the ruling, and IslamQA says the first case is allowed but not advised.

points.title: The Qur'an allows it
points.text: Chaste women of the People of the Book are lawful for Muslim men. Women who worship idols are not.

points.title: He honours her faith
points.text: A Muslim believes in all the messengers and the books they brought, including Moses, Jesus, the Torah and the Gospel. He cannot insult what she holds sacred.

points.title: The reverse is barred
points.text: No Muslim woman may marry a man who does not follow Islam. Scholars are agreed on this.
points.note: Ibn Qudamah, al-Mughni, on marriage to non-Muslims; IslamQA 83736

points.title: The household has a head
points.text: The husband is the protector and provider in the home and shapes the children's upbringing. A husband who denies Islam cannot protect her worship or raise her children in it.

points.title: Faith comes first in a spouse
points.text: The Prophet told believers to choose the religious spouse. So even where the marriage is allowed, scholars often advise against it.

islamqa.title: A Christian woman is saying: Why is it not permissible for a Muslim woman to marry a kitaabi man when the opposite is permitted?

discussion.text: State the rule first. The Qur'an says the chaste women of those given the Scripture before you are lawful for you, when you give them their bridal gift and marry them properly. Chaste is a condition. Women who worship idols are not lawful for a Muslim man. And a Muslim woman may not marry an unbeliever, because she is unlawful for them and they for her. The Qur'an states this for both sexes.

The difference is about whose belief is protected, not whose person is worth more. A man who is Muslim believes in Moses and Jesus and the revelation they were given, so nothing in his home attacks his wife's faith.
