A Christian or Jewish husband does not accept Muhammad or the Qur'an. A Muslim wife would live with someone who denies what she holds most sacred. The rule asks for respect for beliefs to run in both directions.

Islam also gives the husband a role of leadership and care, and children in most families follow the father's guidance. Scholars point to the verse where Allah tells believers to guard themselves and their families. A wife under a husband of another faith, with children being raised in that faith, would be pushed toward giving up her religion or her children's. So the law places the leader of the home in the faith that honours all the prophets.

Honest limits. The permission is not praise. IslamQA discourages it today, quoting Ibn Baz on the fear of great evil, including children being raised as Christians. It is reported that Umar told Hudhayfah to divorce a Jewish wife he had married, fearing others would copy him and choose unwisely. Umar did not call her unlawful. Marrying a religious spouse remains the advice.

The rule does not make the Christian wife second class. The Qur'an says there is no compulsion in religion, so she cannot be forced to convert, and the marriage is described by the same words of love and mercy as any other marriage. Allah made spouses so that they may find rest in each other. A sceptic may still disagree with the rule, but its reason is consistent: a Muslim marriage is meant to protect the faith of both spouses and the children.

topics.title: Belief and Practice
topics.blurb: Why so many rules, and what about good people of other faiths?

questions.q: Do good people of other religions go to Hell?
questions.short: Someone who clearly hears Islam and rejects it is not saved by good deeds alone, because faith in God is the condition for reward in the Hereafter. Someone the message never truly reached is tested on the Day of Judgment, and God is perfectly just.

points.title: Faith is the condition
points.text: Paradise is forbidden to whoever worships others beside God, and no religion but Islam is accepted. Good character is real, but it does not replace knowing your Maker.

points.title: Deeds need a foundation
points.text: Deeds done while denying God become scattered dust in the Hereafter; they are repaid in this world.

points.title: The Prophet's example
points.text: Aisha asked about Ibn Jud'an, who kept family ties and fed the poor before Islam. The Prophet said it would not benefit him, because he never once said: My Lord, forgive my sins on the Day of Judgment.

points.title: No punishment without a message
points.text: God never punishes until a messenger has come. Whoever the message never truly reached is tested on the Day of Judgment.

points.title: Judged by a just God
points.text: Only God knows who was truly reached and who rejected out of stubbornness. Muslims do not pass a verdict on named individuals, apart from those the revelation itself names, such as Abu Lahab.

islamqa.title: Will good deeds avail a person anything if he dies as a kaafir?

discussion.text: The strongest form of the objection is this: a doctor who spends her life healing strangers, and who never met a Muslim, surely cannot burn beside a tyrant. Islam does not deny that her goodness is real, and God says plainly that He wrongs no one, not even by the weight of an atom. The question is what a deed is for. The Qur'an treats worship of God as the purpose of a human life, so a life of kindness that never once turns toward the One who gave it is like a wage claimed from an employer you never worked for.

Islam is also clear about the other side. Scholars distinguish between a person who has heard the message clearly and turned away from it, and a person to whom it never really arrived. For the first, Paradise is forbidden to those who set up partners with God, and a way of life other than submission to Him is not accepted. The Prophet's answer about Ibn Jud'an shows the same principle: kindness done while never seeking God's forgiveness on the Day of Judgment does not carry over into the Hereafter.

For the second group, the Qur'an says God never punishes until a messenger has come, and that messengers were sent so people would have no excuse. Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir of 17:15, records reports that the deaf, the insane, the very senile and those who died in the gap between prophets will be tested on the Day of Judgment: whoever obeys is admitted to Paradise and whoever refuses enters the Fire. Al-Ghazali, in Faysal al-Tafriqa, argued in the same spirit that a person in a distant land who never heard the Prophet's true description is excused, and that Muslims should not lightly declare people lost.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir on 17:15; al-Ghazali, Faysal al-Tafriqa

discussion.text: Honest limits remain. Hearing a message is not the same as being able to see it properly. Someone who only met a distorted picture of Islam, or lived among people who never showed it well, may not have had the truth put before them in a fair way. Only God knows what each heart understood and what was pride. That is why Muslims do not pass a verdict on any named person beyond those the revelation itself names, and why the Qur'an says every record will be laid open and your Lord wrongs no one. A sceptic can reasonably ask whether this is comfortable. The claim is not that it is comfortable, but that judgment belongs to a Judge who is fully just and fully merciful.

questions.q: Isn't Islam just a religion for Arabs?
questions.short: No. The Qur'an addresses all humanity, and the Prophet taught that an Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab except through taqwa. Most Muslims today are not Arabs.

points.title: Sent to all mankind
points.text: The Prophet was sent as a mercy to the worlds and to all people, not to one tribe.

points.title: Worth is piety
points.text: God made nations and tribes so they would know one another, and the noblest is the most righteous.

points.title: The Prophet said so
points.text: In his farewell sermon: an Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, except by taqwa.
points.note: Musnad Ahmad, the farewell sermon; IslamQA 182686

points.title: Non-Arab companions honoured
points.text: Salman was Persian, Bilal Ethiopian and Suhayb from Byzantium, all close to the Prophet.

points.title: Faith went beyond Arabia
points.text: The Prophet put his hand on Salman the Persian and said that if faith were at the Pleiades, men from his people would reach it. Al-Bukhari, of Bukhara, and Abu Hanifa, reported to be of Persian descent, were scholars from outside the Arab lands.

islamqa.title: Is the Arab Muslim better than the non-Arab Muslim?

discussion.text: The objection looks reasonable at first sight: the Qur'an is in Arabic, the Prophet was an Arab, and Mecca is in Arabia. But a message being delivered in one language does not make it owned by one people. Every prophet spoke the tongue of his audience so they could understand him, and the Qur'an makes its own claim about scope: the Prophet was sent as a mercy to all the worlds, to all of humanity, and it calls him a bringer of good news and a warner to everyone.

Next, look at what the text says about status. Humanity is made into peoples and tribes so that we may know one another, and the most honoured with God is the most God-conscious. Differences of language and colour are called signs of God, not ranks. The Prophet's farewell sermon, reported in Musnad Ahmad, states it as a rule: no Arab is above a non-Arab, no non-Arab above an Arab, and no white above a black or black above white, except by taqwa. A religion built to protect one tribe would not teach this.
discussion.note: Musnad Ahmad, the farewell sermon; IslamQA 182686

discussion.text: History points the same way. Around the Prophet stood Salman al-Farisi from Persia, Bilal from Ethiopia and Suhayb from the Byzantine lands. When Surat al-Jumu'ah spoke of others who had not yet joined the believers, the Prophet put his hand on Salman and said that if faith were at the Pleiades, some men from his people would reach it. Classical books such as Ibn Hajar's al-Isabah list the companions by origin, and many were not Arabs.

The numbers today settle the practical question. Arabs are a minority of the world's Muslims, and the largest Muslim countries by population, such as Indonesia, Pakistan and Bangladesh, are not Arab. Scholars like al-Bukhari, who came from Bukhara in Central Asia, shaped the tradition from outside Arabia. There is one honest nuance: Arabic holds a special place, because the Qur'an is recited in its own language in prayer, and the earliest generations were Arab. But that is a matter of preserving one text, not of privileging one people.

questions.q: Why do Muslims pray five times a day? Isn't that excessive?
questions.short: Prayer is the believer's direct meeting with God, and He commanded it five times a day. It takes under an hour in total, and it keeps God present through the whole day.

points.title: Made to worship
points.text: God created humans to worship Him and commanded prayer to remember Him. He knows what our hearts need.

points.title: A reminder through the day
points.text: Prayer keeps a person from indecency and wrongdoing. Spread through the day, it stops forgetfulness building up.

points.title: Short and light
points.text: Each prayer takes a few minutes, and the sick and travellers have concessions.

points.title: Fifty became five
points.text: On the Night Journey fifty prayers were given and reduced to five, with the reward of fifty. Mercy, not burden.

points.title: Some rulings are pure worship
points.text: Some rulings show their reason. The exact number of prayers is accepted from God, like trusting a doctor's prescription without demanding the chemistry.

islamqa.title: Why Do Muslims Pray 5 Times a Day?

discussion.text: The objection is that five prayers a day looks like a heavy demand, and a loving God should not need so much attention. Start with who is asking whom. The Qur'an says God does not need our worship; He created humans to worship Him, and He tells Musa that prayer is for His remembrance. Prayer is therefore less a tax paid to God than a meeting the believer is invited to, and the benefit falls on the one who prays.

Then look at the spacing. Forgetfulness is the ordinary human problem: a person rarely decides to abandon God, they drift. Prayers placed at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night interrupt the drift before it grows. The Qur'an says prayer restrains a person from indecency and wrongdoing, and that prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early part of the night wipes out small wrongs. Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir of 29:45, explains that the prayer restrains because its remembrance of God keeps a person from turning to sin.

On the charge of excess, the practical facts matter. A prayer takes a few minutes, the whole day's worth is well under an hour, and the religion adds concessions. A traveller may shorten the prayer, prayers may be shortened under fear, and rain or illness is recognised as a difficulty. The Qur'an states that God intends ease and not hardship. The Night Journey account tells the same story: fifty prayers were first prescribed, and the Prophet, on Musa's advice, returned to ask for a reduction until five remained, with the reward of fifty.

Finally, an honest limit. The exact number and timing of the prayers is not derived from a chain of reasoning that a sceptic could check; it is accepted as a command. The Qur'an says God is not asked about what He does, while people are asked about what they do. Scholars separate rulings whose reasons are stated from rulings of pure worship, where the believer trusts the Lawgiver, the way a patient follows a prescription without knowing the chemistry. The argument is not that five is mathematically forced. It is that a Creator who knows the human heart set a rhythm that is light, merciful and effective.

questions.q: Why is pork forbidden?
questions.short: Pork is forbidden because God forbade it, and the Qur'an calls it impure. Health harms are a real supporting reason, but Muslims obey the command first.

points.title: An explicit command
points.text: The Qur'an forbids the flesh of swine in four separate places.

points.title: Called impure
points.text: God describes it as rijs, filthy and unfit, and the Prophet forbade even selling swine.

points.title: Good allowed, harmful forbidden
points.text: The Prophet makes lawful what is good and forbids what is bad; pork is in the second group.

points.title: Health reasons exist
points.text: Pigs carry parasites such as tapeworm and trichinella. A supporting point, not the basis.

points.title: Obedience, with mercy
points.text: When God decides a matter, a believer submits. In real necessity, eating it is not a sin.

islamqa.title: Why Is Pork Haram?

discussion.text: A sceptic might say that the ban on pork is a leftover from a desert climate and has no place now. The first thing to see is how the Qur'an itself frames the rule. It forbids the flesh of swine in four separate places, and the reason given is not a health study. It is that this is a command from the One who made lawful and unlawful, and in 6:145 the flesh is called rijs, meaning something filthy.

That is why Muslim scholars say the ruling rests on revelation first, not on medicine. Verse 7:157 says the Prophet makes lawful what is good and forbids what is bad, and Ibn Kathir, on 2:173, notes that scholars agree the ban covers the whole animal. This means a person may find the wisdom, but the ruling does not fall if the wisdom is not found. The Prophet also treated swine as a category for the law of trade, and in the year of the Conquest of Mecca he declared trade in pigs unlawful, together with wine, dead animals and idols.

Is there evidence that pork is bad? IslamQA notes that pigs can carry parasites such as tapeworm and trichinella. Modern cooking and farming reduce these risks a great deal, so a fair reader should not claim that pork is dangerous for everyone today. This is why the health argument is offered as a supporting observation only. If it were the basis, the ban would have to lapse whenever a safe supply appeared, and no Muslim scholar says that.

The deeper reasoning is about what obedience means. A believer who accepts that God is the Creator and is All-Knowing does not demand a laboratory report for each command. The Qur'an says that when God and His Messenger have decided a matter, a believer has no choice in it. This is balanced by mercy: whoever is forced by necessity, not desiring it and not exceeding the need, commits no sin. So the rule is firm, but it does not crush a starving person.

questions.q: Didn't Islam allow slavery?
questions.short: Islam permitted slavery where it already existed everywhere, but never commanded it. It closed nearly every source, gave slaves rights, and made freeing them one of the most rewarded acts.

points.title: Every source but war closed
points.text: Debt, kidnapping and poverty no longer made anyone a slave; classical law kept only war captives and children born to slaves. The Prophet reported that God says He will be against whoever sells a free person and eats the price.

points.title: Freeing is urged
points.text: Freeing a slave is the steep path to righteousness, and the penalty for many sins.

points.title: Captives freed
points.text: Prisoners of war are released as a favour or for ransom. No verse commands enslaving anyone.

points.title: Paths to freedom
points.text: A slave could contract to buy freedom and the master must help; zakah funds free slaves.

points.title: Rights and dignity
points.text: The Prophet said slaves are your brothers: feed them what you eat, clothe them as you dress. Bilal, freed, became the first caller to prayer.
points.note: Bilal as first caller: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah

islamqa.title: Slavery in Islam

discussion.text: The objection is fair and should not be dodged: Islam did not abolish slavery in a single stroke, and the law contains rules about owning people. What a fair reading can show is the direction of the law. Slavery was the normal economic and military system of the seventh century, from Rome and Persia to Arabia. The Qur'an neither commands enslaving anyone nor treats slavery as a goal. It treats it as an existing condition to be narrowed and steadily dissolved.

First, the supply was cut. The Prophet reported that God says He will be against a man who sells a free person and eats the price, which shuts the market in kidnapping. Debt slavery and selling one's own children, which were common in surrounding societies, were not permitted. Classical jurists such as Ibn Qudamah in al-Mughni and al-Nawawi in Rawdat al-Talibin recognised as lawful sources only captives taken in a legitimate war and the children born to slaves. So war captives were not the only source, and the point on this page now says so.
discussion.note: Ibn Qudamah, al-Mughni; al-Nawawi, Rawdat al-Talibin

discussion.text: Second, the exits were opened and paid for. Freeing a slave is called the steep path in Surat al-Balad, and it is the required expiation for accidental killing, for a broken oath and for zihar, a wrongful oath against one's wife. A slave may contract to buy his freedom and the master is told to help, and zakah money is assigned to freeing captives. For prisoners of war, the Qur'an gives the options of release as a favour or ransom.

Third, dignity. The Prophet told his companions that their slaves are their brothers, to be fed and clothed as they themselves are and not burdened beyond their strength. The Qur'an forbids forcing slave women into prostitution. Bilal, freed after being tortured for his faith, became the first caller to prayer, a sign of a former slave holding one of the most honoured public roles.
discussion.note: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, on Bilal and the first adhan

discussion.text: Honest limits: the law did not ban ownership outright, and in practice treatment across Muslim history was uneven, sometimes falling well short of these ideals. The reply a Muslim gives is that the sources push consistently toward freedom, that today's treaties and states have ended the practice, and that scholars widely hold that the conditions which made it lawful, a legitimate war and its captives, no longer apply. The argument is not that history was perfect. It is that the revelation aimed at its end.

questions.q: Isn't praying toward the Kaaba and kissing the Black Stone idol worship?
questions.short: Muslims pray to Allah alone, and the Kaaba is only the direction, like the centre of a circle that unites them. The Prophet removed every idol from it, and Umar said as he kissed the Black Stone that he knew it was only a stone that cannot help or harm. Kissing it is following the Prophet, not asking it for anything.

points.title: Prayer is to Allah alone
points.text: Every prayer includes the words: You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help. East and west belong to Allah, wherever the body faces.

points.title: A direction, not a god
points.text: Righteousness is not in turning your face east or west. The Kaaba gives all Muslims one point to face so they pray as one body.

points.title: The Prophet cleared it of idols
points.text: When Makkah was opened, he entered and struck the 360 idols around the Kaaba with a stick, saying truth has come and falsehood has vanished.

points.title: Umar on the Black Stone
points.text: Umar kissed it and said: I know you are a stone that cannot benefit or harm; had I not seen the Prophet kiss you, I would not.

points.title: Built by Ibrahim for Allah
points.text: Ibrahim and Ismail raised the House by Allah's order, to be kept pure for those who circle it and pray. Following his rites is obedience.

islamqa.title: Why Do Muslims Kiss the Black Stone?

discussion.text: Start with what the Qur'an calls idol worship. The idolaters said of their idols that they served them only so they would bring them nearer to Allah. That means praying to them, asking them for help and offering to them. No Muslim prays to the Kaaba, asks it for anything or offers it anything. Every prayer says: You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help. And the Qur'an says east and west belong to Allah, so a prayer is not tied to a place.

Why then face one building? Think of a circle. A billion people cannot all stand in the same place, but they can face the same centre, and then they are one body. No one thinks the centre of a circle is what they are worshipping. The first direction in Islam was Jerusalem; then it changed to the Kaaba, and some people mocked. The Qur'an said the change was a test of who follows the Messenger, and it also says righteousness is not in the direction itself.

The history of the House is the opposite of idolatry. The Qur'an says Ibrahim and Ismail raised its foundations, and Allah told them to keep it pure for those who circle it, stand in it and bow in prayer. Later, idols were placed around it. When the Prophet took Makkah he did not leave one. He struck them with a stick, saying the truth has come. The one house dedicated to the one God was cleared of every other object of worship.

The Black Stone is part of the rites of Hajj, not a thing to be prayed to. The Prophet kissed it, and the Companions did as he did. Umar made the meaning plain in front of the crowd: you are a stone, you cannot help or harm, and I only kiss you because I saw the Prophet do it. Scholars take his words as the rule. It is a sign of obedience, and asking the stone for blessing or protection is not permitted. A pilgrim who cannot get near may simply point toward it.
discussion.note: IslamQA 118085; al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, on Umar's words

discussion.text: Honest limits. From outside, gestures like circling and kissing can look like idol worship, and it is fair for a sceptic to say so. The test the Qur'an gives is where the heart and the request are directed. A Muslim in tawaf makes du'a to Allah, and a Muslim who believed the stone itself had power would be breaking his own religion. Kissing something out of obedience or love does not mean it is worshipped, as a person may kiss a child or a parent's hand.

questions.q: If Islam is the truth, why are there so many sects?
questions.short: The Prophet told us his community would split, and the Qur'an forbids it. Most of the splitting is honest disagreement over details of law among scholars who share the same core, and this is not a sect. Real deviations exist, and every group has to argue from the same preserved book, which is what lets them be corrected.

points.title: The Prophet foretold it
points.text: He said the Jews and Christians split into many groups, and that his community would split into seventy-three.

points.title: Allah forbids dividing
points.text: Hold firmly to Allah's rope together and do not divide. The same command was given to Noah, Ibrahim, Moses and Jesus.

points.title: Splitting follows knowledge
points.text: Earlier peoples split not because the truth was unclear, but after clear proof came to them, out of rivalry. Division is a human failing, not a fault in the message.

points.title: The way out is named
points.text: Asked which group was safe, he said it is what I and my Companions are upon. He told them to hold fast to his Sunnah and that of the rightly guided caliphs.

points.title: Honest difference is not a sect
points.text: Two groups of Companions read one order differently, and the Prophet blamed neither. A judge who tries hard and errs still earns a reward.

islamqa.title: Which Group Is the Saved One?

discussion.text: The question assumes that if a message is true, everyone will agree about it. History shows the opposite: people divide over the clearest teachings, in every religion and every science. The Qur'an says this directly. The earlier communities did not divide until knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves. So the fact of division does not count against the message. It shows what people do with a message, and Muslims are warned against doing the same.

The Prophet warned of it in advance. In the report of Abu Hurayrah, he said the Jews and the Christians each split into seventy-odd groups and his community would split into seventy-three. In the version of Abdullah ibn Amr, all but one are in the Fire, and that one is those on what he and his Companions were upon. Scholars grade the last part differently: al-Albani calls it hasan, Zubair Ali Zai calls it weak, and al-Bukhari and Muslim did not include it.
discussion.note: Grades of Tirmidhi 2641 as recorded in the hadith database

discussion.text: Distinguish law from belief. The four schools of law differ on things like details of prayer or purity, but they share the same creed and the same pillars. The Companions themselves differed in this way, as when one party prayed Asr on the road and the other waited until Banu Qurayza, and the Prophet blamed neither. IslamQA states that following an accepted school is not one of the seventy-three sects.

On belief, the Prophet said a group of his community would stay upright on Allah's command, not harmed by those who oppose them. IslamQA names them as Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah, those who hold to the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the consensus of scholars. It adds that most groups who went astray are still Muslim, quoting Ibn Taymiyyah, though extreme sects fall outside Islam. The Qur'an gives the method for disputes: return them to Allah and the Messenger.

Honest limits. This answer does not give a sceptic what he may want, a single visible authority who settles every dispute. After the Prophet, Islam has none. What it has is one preserved text that every group must argue from, and a long tradition of scholars who correct each other with evidence. That is why a mistaken group can be answered from the book they too accept, and why the Qur'an, kept safe by Allah, is the means of reform.

questions.q: Aren't Islamic punishments like cutting off hands barbaric?
questions.short: The fixed penalties cover only a few crimes and apply only when proof is close to certain: a free confession or clear eyewitnesses, with no doubt at all. Any doubt cancels them, and only a judge may apply them. Umar did not cut the thief's hand in the famine year, since need makes the theft doubtful.

points.title: Few crimes, hard proof
points.text: Adultery needs four witnesses who saw the act itself. Someone who accuses without them is himself lashed eighty times.

points.title: Theft has conditions
points.text: The hand is cut only for secret taking of stored goods above a set value, a quarter dinar. It needs two witnesses or a confession.

points.title: Doubt cancels the penalty
points.text: The Prophet tried to turn away a man who confessed, asking if he had only kissed her. Scholars rule that doubt averts the fixed penalties.
points.note: Ibn Qudamah, al-Mughni, on averting hudud by doubt

points.title: Need stops the penalty
points.text: In the famine year Umar did not cut off the hand of a thief. Hunger makes the theft doubtful and calls for relief first.
points.note: Ibn al-Qayyim, I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in, on the year of famine

points.title: The same law for all
points.text: The Prophet refused to excuse a noble woman from the law and said nations were destroyed when they spared the great and punished the weak.

islamqa.title: The hadd punishment for theft

discussion.text: The picture in people's minds is a hand, but these penalties are a small part of Islamic law and the last layer of it. First comes prevention: honest earnings, zakat for the poor, a ban on alcohol and on the ways that lead to adultery. The penalty is for a person who breaks all that in the open and is proven guilty. The Qur'an says that in fair retribution there is life for you, and the aim is protection of life, property and family for all.

Now the proof. The penalty for adultery needs four witnesses who saw the act, and they must agree. That is close to impossible, unless it is done openly, which is exactly what the law is aimed at. A person who accuses and fails is lashed eighty times. Even a confession is questioned: when Ma'iz confessed, the Prophet asked if he had only kissed her or looked, and made him say plainly what he had done. The law is built to make conviction hard, not easy.

For theft, the hand is cut only when the thief secretly takes goods kept in a safe place worth at least a quarter dinar, has no claim on it and was not driven by need, and is proven by two witnesses or by confession. Umar did not apply the penalty in the famine year, and scholars ruled that hunger and need make the theft doubtful. The thief may also repent and return the goods before the case reaches the judge, and Allah accepts repentance.

Only a judge in a Muslim state may apply the penalties, never a family or a crowd. The law is the same for high and low: the Prophet told Usama not to plead for the noble woman of Makhzum who stole, and said nations before were destroyed for sparing the great. Yet he also urged people to forgive between themselves before a case reaches him. He said whoever is punished in this world, it is an expiation for that sin.

Honest limits. Scholars today differ on how these penalties apply where courts and care for the poor fall short. The doubt rule and the famine ruling show that the law asks for fair proof and relief from need first. A sceptic may still find the penalties harsh. Muslims accept them as the law of the One who knows best what protects people, and note how strict the proof is.
discussion.note: Ibn Taymiyyah, al-Siyasa al-Shar'iyya, on the purpose of the fixed penalties

questions.q: What does Islam say about homosexuality?
questions.short: Islam forbids the act, as it forbids all sex outside marriage between a man and a woman. Passing thoughts that are not acted on or spoken are forgiven, and Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Punishment is for a court alone, with strict proof, and Muslims are told never to mock or spy on anyone.

points.title: The act is forbidden
points.text: The Qur'an tells the story of Lut's people and calls the act a transgression. Muslims do not hold it lawful.

points.title: The Sunnah agrees
points.text: A hadith from Ibn Abbas treats it as a grave crime. Al-Albani graded it sahih. Scholars differ on the penalty, but not on the ban.

points.title: Passing thoughts are forgiven
points.text: Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. The Prophet said Allah has forgiven his people the thoughts that come to them, as long as they are not acted on or spoken. IslamQA 2104 speaks only about the act, so this point rests on that hadith and verse.

points.title: Chastity is asked of all
points.text: Every unmarried Muslim, whatever the desire, is asked to guard chastity, marry if able, and fast if not. The one who says 'I fear Allah' and refuses is praised.

points.title: Courts only, and strict proof
points.text: Only a judge may act, and only on strict proof. The Qur'an sets four witnesses before anyone may accuse another of unchastity, and lashes those who accuse without them. Spying, mocking and exposing people are forbidden.

islamqa.title: Is Homosexuality a Sin?

discussion.text: Say the position plainly. In Islam, sex is lawful only within marriage between a man and a woman. The act between two men or two women is forbidden, as is any sex outside marriage. The Qur'an tells the story of the people of Lut and calls what they did a transgression. This is a religious ruling, and Muslims hold it whatever the surrounding culture says. It is one rule within a wider law of chastity that applies to everybody.

Now the part that is often missed. There is a difference between a thought and a deed. The Prophet said Allah has forgiven his community the thoughts that pass through them, as long as they do not speak or act on them, and the Qur'an says Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. On that basis a passing inclination that is held back is not counted as the act, and restraint is rewarded. IslamQA 2104 speaks only about the act and does not discuss inclination. The Prophet praised the man who refused an invitation to sin, saying he feared Allah.

On punishment, the classical scholars did not agree. The majority held death, relying on the hadith of Ibn Abbas, which al-Albani graded sahih; others said it is treated like adultery; Abu Hanifa said the judge decides a lesser penalty. Whatever the view, only a judge in a Muslim state may decide, and no private person may harm another. The Qur'an itself sets a high bar of proof before anyone may accuse another of unchastity.
discussion.note: IslamQA 38622, which lists the three views

discussion.text: How Muslims must treat people. The Qur'an forbids mocking others, since the one mocked may be better in Allah's sight, and forbids spying on their private faults. A person who sins in private is told to keep it hidden and repent, and repentance is never closed: Allah forgives all sins for those who turn to Him. Cruelty, hatred and humiliation toward a person are not part of Islamic teaching, even while the act itself is held to be wrong.

Honest limits. This is a real hardship: a Muslim with such an attraction is asked for a lifetime of restraint and cannot have the partner he might choose. Islam asks the same restraint of every unmarried person, and of every married person toward everyone else. It does not say it is easy. The Qur'an says man was created weak, and the answer given is patience, fasting, good company and the promise of reward. A sceptic may reject the ruling, but he should see that it is directed at the act, and not at people.
discussion.note: Ibn al-Qayyim, 'Uddat al-Sabirin, on patience against desire
